blocks.text: So much on Noah's raven according to the Hebrews. The Greeks, however, put it very differently: their version appears to deny the very thing that Moses expressly asserts, namely that the raven came back. For it has Ἐξελθὼν οὐκ ἀνέστρεψεν [Exelthōn ouk anestrepsen], Having gone out (from the ark, the raven) did not return, for the Hebrew ויצא יצוא ושוב, And it went out, going out and returning. The Syriac likewise has ܘܢܦܩ ܡܦܩ ܘܠܐ ܗܦܟ, And it went out, going out, and did not return. And Jerome: Which went out and did not return. And two Arabic manuscripts which I saw in Sweden have لم يعون [lam yaʿūn] it did not return, or فلم يعد [fa-lam yaʿud] and it did not return. But the former is plainly rendered from the Greek version, the latter from the Syriac. The early doctors follow the same reading: Hilary, Arnobius and Pseudo-Jerome on Psalm 146; the genuine Jerome in the Dialogue against the Luciferians, chapter 8; Ambrose, On Noah and the Ark, chapter 17; Sulpicius Severus, History, book 1; Augustine on Genesis, book 1, Question 13, and elsewhere; Chrysostom on Genesis, book 2. Also Eutychius of Alexandria, p. 40: فذهب الغراب ولم يرجع [fa-dhahaba al-ghurāb wa-lam yarjiʿ] And the raven went away, and did not return. In short, all the ancients whom I have been able to come across, except Procopius alone, who does not admit the negation. Hence a twofold question arises: first, where this difference of readings originated; [II, 802] second, which reading is true and to be preferred to the other. To the first many reply that the Hebrews and the Greeks can very well be reconciled, since both statements are truly made: that the raven returned and that the raven did not return. For it returned to the ark, or onto the ark, but did not return into the ark. This answer is empty. For neither reading says that the raven returned or did not return into the ark or onto the ark; rather, one of them says simply that the raven returned, the other that it did not return, which are flatly contrary. If someone rendered the words of Moses, Gen. XXII, 1. God tested Abraham, as God did not test Abraham, would he not be a false translator, even though it is in some sense true that God did not test Abraham, namely in the sense in which James said ^{a)} that God tempts no one? Moreover, although the Hebrew text does not expressly say that the raven returned into the ark, it is nevertheless plainly implied. For the words run thus: It went out, going out and returning, until, etc. That is, it often went out and often returned. And in order to go out of the ark often, it had necessarily to go back into it often. For no one goes out of a house who has not gone into it. According to others the Hebrew שוב [col. 211] means not only to return but also to recede, as in verse 3 of this very chapter: וישבו המים מעל הארץ הלוך ושוב, And the waters returned from the face of the earth, going and returning, that is, they receded steadily. And in the same way, they say, the raven went out, going out from the ark, ושוב, and returning, that is, receding. And to recede from the ark, they assert, is the same as not returning to it. But neither is this answer adequate. For whatever they say, שוב properly means to return. Even when the waters are said to have returned from the face of the earth, they are said to have returned because they had previously submerged it and were withdrawing from the face of the earth to their natural place, that is, into the sea, etc. Moreover, שוב is not taken in the sense of receding unless the particle מן, that is, from or out of, is added, which nowhere appears here. Finally, these words do not hang together: The raven went out, going out and receding, until the waters had dried up. For the raven went out on the eleventh day of the eleventh month, Gen. VIII, 5. 6., and the waters dried up only at the beginning of the following year, Gen. VIII, 13., that is, fifty days after the raven went out. No one would say that the raven kept receding from the ark during that whole time. But granting, without conceding, that the Hebrew words could be rendered thus, The raven went out, going out and receding, the Greek version, The raven having gone out did not return, would still differ greatly from them. For to go away and recede from somewhere over a fifty days' journey is not the same as to go away from there and not return before the fiftieth day. Others hold that the Jews removed the negation from the Hebrew text; they are refuted by the agreement of the Samaritan codex with the Hebrew. Moreover the two Chaldees, Jonathan and Onkelos, have here ונפק מפק ותאיב. And the Samaritan translator has ࠅࠍࠐࠒ ࠌࠐࠅࠒ ࠅࠕࠁ And it went out, going out and returning. And the Arabic edited at Paris, [II, 803] فجعل يخرج ويرجع [fa-jaʿala yakhruju wa-yarjiʿu] And it kept going out and coming back. And Erpenianus, وخرج خارجا وراجعا [wa-kharaja khārijan wa-rājiʿan] And it went out, going out and returning. Josephus also, Antiqu. book 1, ch. 4: πρὸς Νῶχον ἐπανῆλθε [pros Nōchon epanēlthe], It returned to Noah. Moreover, in Bereshit Rabbah and in the Agudda, which are very ancient books of the Hebrews, this passage reads exactly as in our codices. Finally, I am entirely convinced that Jerome read it thus, and that the Hebrew Questions read wrongly: „And of the raven it is said otherwise (in the Hebrew text): And he sent out the raven, and it went out, going out and not returning“. For one should read going out and returning. For if you read and not returning, why does he assert that the Hebrew text says something different from the Greek? This observation of the bishop of Chisamus is entirely true. Nor indeed did the Jews have any reason to corrupt that passage, since it makes no difference to them whether the raven is believed to have returned or not. Finally, there are those who think the negation was inserted into the Greek codices, either deliberately or through the carelessness of scribes; neither of these is at all likely. Not the former, because just as the Hebrews had no reason to remove the negation from the Hebrew text, so the Greek translators had no reason to add it to their version. Nor the latter, because if you take the negation out of the Greek words (Ἐξελθὼν οὐκ ἀνέστρεψεν, ἕως τοῦ ξηρανθῆναι τὸ ὕδωρ [Exelthōn ouk anestrepsen, heōs tou xēranthēnai to hydōr], Having gone out it did not return until the waters had dried up), the whole structure of the sentence falls apart, and it will make no sense at all: Having gone out it returned until the waters had dried up. Since, therefore, this version is framed in words from which the negation can in no way be absent, it is clear that it was written by the translators themselves, not slipped in and inserted into the text by scribal error.
